citations.narrative:
The public was having contact with the animals and there was not a readily identifiable attendant present at the time of
the interactions. In the central part of the walk-through area, members of the public were observed petting and feeding
animals at a feeding station in an enclosure housing three emu, eight eland and twelve fallow deer. Allowing public
contact without an attendant present can lead to injuries to the animals and/or the public. The facility needs to have a
responsible, knowledgeable, and readily identifiable employee or attendant present at all times during periods of public
contact to ensure the safety of the animals and the members of the public.
To be corrected by 7-1-2026.

The refrigerator located in a primate lock out storage area had various chemicals stored inside with the food. Chemical
substances that contaminate food may cause harm to the animals.
Supplies of food and bedding must be stored in a manner that protects the supplies from spoilage, contamination, and
vermin infestation. Substances that are toxic to the nonhuman primates but that are required for normal husbandry
practices must not be stored in food storage and preparation areas but may be stored in cabinets in the animal areas.
To be corrected by 7-1-2026.

None of the primate cages at the facility have an effective means to cool the sheltered portions of the enclosures. Without
appropriate and effective cooling mechanisms, there is no practical way to maintain internal shelter temperatures at an
appropriate level.
At the time of inspection, the temperature for the sheltered portion of the housing facility for four brown lemurs was
measured at 91° F. The ambient high temperature that day was 93 F. Excessively hot shelter structures can negatively
impact the well-being of the enclosed primates and could prevent the animals from freely using their shelters.
The sheltered part of sheltered housing facilities must be sufficiently heated and cooled when necessary to protect the
nonhuman primates from temperature extremes, and to provide for their health and well-being. The ambient temperature
in the sheltered part of the facility must not fall below 45 °F (7.2 °C) for more than 4 consecutive hours when nonhuman
primates are present, and must not rise above 85°F (29.5 °C) for more than 4 consecutive hours when nonhuman
primates are present, unless temperatures above 85 °F (29.5 °C) are approved by the attending veterinarian, in
accordance with generally accepted husbandry practices. The ambient temperature must be maintained at a level that
ensures the health and well-being of the species housed, as directed by the attending veterinarian, in accordance with
generally accepted professional and husbandry practices.
To be corrected by July 15, 2026.

The enclosure for a female howler monkey, Juliet, had numerous areas of rust within reach of the animal. The rusted
areas were deeply pitted and flaking. Excessive rust can compromise the structural strength of an enclosure as well as
prevent adequate cleaning and sanitation.
Housing facilities for nonhuman primates must be designed and constructed so that they are structurally sound for the
species of nonhuman primates housed in them and enable all surfaces in contact with nonhuman primates to be readily
cleaned and sanitized or replaced when worn or soiled.
To be corrected by 7-10-2026.

citations.desc: Environment enhancement to promote psychological well-being.
citations.narrative:
Three cotton-top tamarins were housed without sufficient environmental enrichment. The cages lacked sufficient perches
or resting platforms and contained no environmental enrichment. One of the tamarins was observed using the food bowl
as a perch.
The physical environment in the primary enclosures must be enriched by providing means of expressing noninjurious
species-typical activities. Species differences should be considered when determining the type or methods of enrichment.
Examples of environmental enrichments include providing perches, swings, mirrors, and other increased cage
complexities; providing objects to manipulate; varied food items; using foraging or task-oriented feeding methods; and
providing interaction with the care giver or other familiar and knowledgeable person consistent with personnel safety
precautions.
To be corrected by 7-1-2026.

An open bucket of feed was observed in the lockout/storage area for several non-human primate enclosures. Numerous
flies were on the container and crawling on the food. Pests can contaminate food with disease causing organisms that
could be harmful to the animals.
The diet for nonhuman primates must be appropriate for the species, size, age, and condition of the animal, and for the
conditions in which the nonhuman primate is maintained, according to generally accepted professional and husbandry
practices and nutritional standards. The food must be clean, wholesome, and palatable to the animals.
To be corrected by 7-1-2026.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
Rodents were observed running into a large, separated section of wood roofing directly above an olive baboon. The
opening was approximately four feet long and one-two inches in width. Rodents are a potential source of contamination to
the enclosed animals.
An effective program for control of insects, external parasites affecting nonhuman primates, and birds and mammals that
are pests, must be established and maintained so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals and reduce
contamination by pests in animal areas.
To be corrected by 7-1-2026.

There were multiple areas of the facility in need of repair and maintenance. All structures must be maintained in good
repair to help protect the enclosed animals.
-The enclosure for the male white rhino had a section of woven wire that was crumpled, had several holes, and numerous
sharp points. The sharp points could cause injury to the rhino, and the damaged woven wire may be a source of
entrapment.
-The enclosure housing two otters had a large drain near the center of the pool that had a protection cover with large
openings that could entrap an animal.
-The enclosure for two pygmy hippos had an electrical cord with a plug in connection that was suspended approximately
two feet above the pool water. The cord was loosely attached to a metal rod with a frayed rope. Unprotected electrical
cords that contact water may cause serious injury to the enclosed animals.
The indoor and outdoor housing facilities shall be structurally sound and shall be maintained in good repair to protect the
animals from injury and to contain the animals.
To be corrected by 7-3-2026.

A single prairie dog has been held in a small enclosure for approximately four months. The enclosure does not appear to
be an appropriate size to provide the prairie dog with necessary living and exercise space. The animal appeared
depressed and inactive but became extremely animated and excited when temporarily removed from the enclosure to
interact with a handler.
Enclosures shall be constructed and maintained so as to provide sufficient space to allow each animal to make normal
postural and social adjustments with adequate freedom of movement. Inadequate space may be indicated by evidence of
malnutrition, poor condition, debility, stress, or abnormal behavior patterns.
To be corrected by 7-1-2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
Michael Tygart, VETERINARY MEDICAL OFFICER n
